text: @ykilcher I think you're confusing "superhuman" with "above-average". There were definitely *profitable* PLO bots years ago. But there's a huge difference between that and being better than the best professional humans.

@Miles_Brundage I remember Demis Hassabis once talking about how people told him after AlphaGo that it was obvious a computer could beat humans at Go. It's natural to adjust to the "new normal" and lose track of how incredible the pace of progress in AI has been.

author: polynoamial
text: @Miles_Brundage @cosmosPixelado My guess is DM was getting severely diminishing returns from throwing more ppl/TPUs at it, and the project was already super expensive. Also, the unexploitable part is extremely hard and nobody knows how to go about it in a game like SC2

author: polynoamial
text: @Miles_Brundage @cosmosPixelado To be clear, I think AlphaStar is incredible, it's clearly at a grandmaster level, and they never claimed it was superhuman. I just think it's important for the AI community to recognize the limitations of current AI techniques.

author: polynoamial
text: @Miles_Brundage @cosmosPixelado I hate to be *that guy*, but AlphaStar, while incredibly strong, isn't superhuman. It couldn't beat top humans and is highly exploitable. SC2 is still a difficult research problem, but sadly at this point doing it properly wouldn't result in much recognition

text: @ykilcher The first part of your tweet is correct but the second part isn't. How do you estimate opponent hand ranges? How do you balance your actions so your own range is optimal? And how do you learn all of this from scratch? Those are the hard parts, and that's more than just statistics

author: polynoamial
text: 9) I'll close by recommending this PhD apps guide: https://t.co/huCalClPLy . It's a bit harsh, but it helped me a ton when I was debating going for a PhD. I was on the fence about applying and thought there was a good chance I'd drop out, but I ended up loving grad school. (9/9)

author: polynoamial
text: 8) Some people advise against working because "once you get used to the money, you'll find it hard to leave". That's a bad reason. There's nothing wrong with NOT doing a PhD. If you're happy and don't want to do 5-6 years of low-pay self-directed research in a PhD, then don't.

author: polynoamial
text: 7) Some folks asked if working hurts your chances at a top PhD program. For the reasons above, I think it's the opposite (would love to hear from faculty on this). But if you're worried about stale letters, apply to PhDs right after graduating and then defer your start by a year.

author: polynoamial
text: 6) Once you start a PhD, any extended break to work on non-research will hurt your chances at a postdoc/faculty/tenure position. Working before grad school is the safest time to try something different. It's nice to see what life is like outside the ivory tower for a bit. (6/9)

author: polynoamial
text: 5) If you're able to do research in industry (for example, as an engineer at Facebook AI Research) and work with PhDs, you could get valuable letters that will improve your grad school application. I had zero undergrad research experience, so this is what got me into grad school.

author: polynoamial
text: 4) Working gives you MONEY. Pay off loans and save up, and you'll be able to live a more comfortable and enjoyable life while in grad school. Plus, you'll be able to make decisions about which program to attend without worrying as much about short-term finances. (4/9)

author: polynoamial
text: 3) Working gives you maturity that will help you adjust to grad school. A PhD is a highly self-directed full-time job. I know many students that went straight from undergrad to a PhD and had trouble managing their time. Working a full-time job will help prepare you for that.

author: polynoamial
text: 2) Working gives you skills and experience that will help in your academic career. Work at a tech company and you'll become a better coder, which is invaluable in CS grad school. (2/9)

author: polynoamial
text: 1) PhD program dropout rates are high: 30-50%. That's not because people "don't make the cut". It's because they realize they'd rather do something else. Working gives you perspective and helps you decide what you want. It made me realize I'd rather do a CS PhD than an Econ PhD.

author: polynoamial
text: This generated more discussion than I expected, so here's a thread on why working before grad school is a good idea. (0/9)

quoted.text: Everyone I know that worked for a couple years before starting grad school is glad they did it.

author: polynoamial
text: @catherineols @ChrKroer @cjmaddison I think that's unlikely, but for anyone worried about stale letters: you can defer grad school after acceptance. So you could apply right after senior year (and get even better letters from undergrad advisors), then defer acceptance and work for another year for 2 years total.

author: polynoamial
text: @ChrKroer @catherineols @cjmaddison If I were a professor, I think I'd be *more* likely to take on someone that has a couple years of work experience. Grad school is more like a full-time job than it is like undergrad, and for some the transition from undergrad to grad can be tough.
